did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah describes a change in the Lord’s attitude: after the anger turns away, comfort follows, and the response is thanksgiving.
Did you know? The expression “On that day” is repeated in the chapter and presents these events as part of a special day of salvation and thanksgiving.
Did you know? In this verse, the Lord is described as “God my salvation,” and the speaker expresses trust in Him, saying, “I will trust and not be afraid.”
Did you know? The verse also calls the Lord “my strength and my song,” meaning the source of strength and song, and concludes that the Lord has become the speaker’s salvation.
Did you know? Salvation is compared to springs of water: the people draw from them “with joy,” presenting salvation as a source of happiness and refreshment.
Did you know? The people are called not only to give thanks to the Lord and call on His name, but also to proclaim His deeds among the nations and make known that His name is exalted.
Did you know? Singing to the Lord is connected with the fact that He has acted gloriously; according to the verse, knowledge of His deeds is made known throughout the earth.
Did you know? Zion is called to shout and sing for joy because “great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel”—His presence among her is the source of her joy.
